title: The Silk Road: How Trade Connected Two Worlds

chapters.title: A road that was never one road

scenes.purpose: Hook: one bolt of silk and everything else the routes carried.

visual.title: A bolt of silk crosses a continent
visual.statement: For over 1,500 years, caravans linked China and the Mediterranean, carrying far more than cloth.

narration.text: Picture a bolt of Chinese silk draped over a Roman senator's shoulders, two thousand years ago.
It had crossed deserts, mountains and empires to get there.
Yet almost no one carried it the whole way.
Along the same routes moved silk, spices and horses,
religions and inventions,
and, at times, deadly diseases.

scenes.purpose: Define the Silk Road and correct the idea of a single road.

visual.title: What was the Silk Road?
visual.definition: A shifting network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean.
visual.example: The name was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

narration.text: The name Silk Road sounds ancient, but it is surprisingly modern.
A German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, coined it in 1877.
And it was never a single road.
It was a shifting web of tracks, oasis towns and sea lanes, linking China to Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean.

scenes.purpose: Show the main overland route across Eurasia.

narration.text: The main overland routes began in Chang'an, the capital of Han China.
Caravans headed west to Dunhuang, the last Chinese outpost before the desert.
They skirted the great Taklamakan Desert to reach Kashgar.
Beyond the Pamir mountains lay Samarkand, a rich trading city.
The routes ran on through Merv and across Persia,
to Antioch and other cities near the Mediterranean coast.
From there, ships carried the goods on to Rome.

scenes.purpose: Give the scale of the network in distance and time.

visual.title: A network on a vast scale

stats.label: overland, from China to the Mediterranean
of trade, on and off, from about 130 BC

visual.note: Distances are approximate; the routes shifted over the centuries.

narration.text: End to end, the overland journey covered roughly four thousand miles.
Few caravans ever traveled all of it.
And the routes stayed busy, on and off, for more than fifteen hundred years.

scenes.purpose: Explain the military problem that opened the routes.

visual.title: An empire in need of allies
visual.statement: In the second century BC, Han China faced constant raids from nomadic horsemen to the north.

narration.text: The story begins with a problem, not a product.
Around 140 BC, Han China suffered raids from powerful nomads on the northern steppe.
Emperor Wu wanted allies who could strike those nomads from the west.
He also wanted something China lacked: big, strong war horses.

scenes.purpose: Tell Zhang Qian's journey as the opening of the routes.

events.label: Zhang Qian sets out to find allies
Escapes after a decade as a captive
Returns with news of new lands
Han armies march west for horses

narration.text: In 138 BC, the emperor sent an envoy named Zhang Qian west to find allies.
The nomads captured him and held him for about ten years.
He escaped and kept going, reaching the kingdoms of Central Asia.
He came home in 126 BC without an alliance, but with something better: knowledge.
He described rich cities, new crops and the famous horses of the Ferghana Valley.
Within a generation, Han armies marched west to win those horses.

scenes.purpose: Contrast what each end of the routes wanted.

narration.text: Trade grew because each end of the routes had what the other craved.
China wanted horses, allies and influence, plus luxuries like glass and precious metals.
Buyers in the West wanted Chinese silk above all, with spices and gems picked up along the way.

scenes.purpose: Show relay trade through many middlemen.

narration.text: Very few people traveled the whole route.
Silk left workshops in China,
changed hands in oasis markets along the way,
passed through Central Asian and Persian middlemen,
and finally reached buyers in the Roman world.
Every handoff added a profit, so prices soared with distance.

scenes.purpose: Define the caravanserai.

visual.title: A roof for the night
visual.definition: A walled roadside inn with a courtyard, where caravans could rest, trade and shelter their animals.
visual.example: Ruins of caravanserais still stand across Iran, Turkey and Central Asia.

narration.text: On the road, travelers depended on the caravanserai.
It was a walled inn where merchants could sleep, swap news and protect their animals and goods.
Many were built in later centuries, and their ruins still dot Iran, Turkey and Central Asia.

scenes.purpose: Give a feel for caravan speed and loads.

visual.title: The ship of the desert

stats.label: of cargo on one Bactrian camel
for a caravan on a good day

visual.note: Typical figures; loads and speeds varied with terrain and season.

narration.text: The workhorse of the desert was the two-humped Bactrian camel.
One animal could carry about two hundred kilograms of cargo.
A caravan might cover thirty kilometers on a good day.
At that pace, crossing the whole network would take many months.

scenes.purpose: Show how caravans skirted the Taklamakan Desert.

narration.text: The hardest stretch was the Taklamakan, a sea of shifting sand in what is now western China.
Caravans left Dunhuang and kept to the desert's edges.
The northern track ran through oases like Turpan,
and Kucha, watered by snowmelt from the mountains.
A southern track hugged the other side of the desert.
The two met again at Kashgar, gateway to the high passes of the Pamirs.

scenes.purpose: Convey the dangers of the journey.

visual.title: Every crossing was a gamble
visual.statement: Merchants risked their fortunes, and often their lives, on each journey.

narration.text: Every crossing was a gamble.
Sandstorms could bury tracks and wells overnight, and water ran short.
Bandits raided caravans, and local rulers charged heavy tolls.
In the mountains, passes over four thousand meters high brought bitter cold.

scenes.purpose: Explain why Rome prized silk.

visual.title: A fabric fit for emperors
visual.statement: Romans had no idea how silk was made; some writers thought it was combed from leaves.

narration.text: In Rome, silk caused a sensation.
It was light and shimmering, unlike any cloth made in Europe.
Romans had no idea how it was made; some writers believed it was combed from leaves.
Its rarity made it enormously expensive,
and wearing it announced wealth and power.

scenes.purpose: Hear a Roman complaint about the cost of eastern luxuries.

visual.title: Rome counts the cost
visual.quote: India, the Seres, and the Arabian Peninsula withdraw from our empire one hundred millions of sesterces every year.
visual.author: Pliny the Elder

narration.text: Some Romans worried about the bill.
The writer Pliny the Elder complained that eastern luxuries drained the empire's wealth.
India, the Seres, and the Arabian Peninsula withdraw from our empire one hundred millions of sesterces every year.
The Seres were the silk people: the Roman name for the Chinese.

scenes.purpose: Show how silk is made, the secret China guarded.

narration.text: China guarded the secret of silk for centuries.
Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves,
then each spins a cocoon from one continuous thread, often hundreds of meters long.
Workers soak the cocoons in hot water to loosen that thread,
and reel several strands together into silk yarn.

scenes.purpose: Tell how the secret of silk reached Byzantium.

visual.title: The great silk heist
visual.statement: Around 552 AD, a Byzantine historian wrote, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople.

narration.text: The secret finally slipped out in the sixth century.
According to the historian Procopius, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople inside hollow canes.
The emperor Justinian soon had silk workshops of his own.
China's monopoly was over, but the routes stayed busy.

scenes.purpose: Introduce ideas as the routes' biggest cargo.

visual.title: Ideas traveled too
visual.statement: Merchants, monks and pilgrims carried faiths, inventions and art along the same tracks.

narration.text: The Silk Road's most important cargo may have been ideas.
Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China.
Papermaking traveled the other way, from China toward the Islamic world and Europe.
Music, painting styles and even recipes moved with the caravans.

scenes.purpose: Trace Buddhism's path into China.

narration.text: Buddhism began in northern India, around the fifth century BC.
It flourished in Gandhara, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Monks and merchants carried it into the oasis towns of the Silk Road.
At Dunhuang, believers later carved hundreds of cave temples, filled with paintings.
By the first century AD, Buddhism had reached the Han heartland around Luoyang.

scenes.purpose: Follow paper from China to Europe.

events.label: First paper mills in Europe, in Spain

narration.text: Take paper.
Around 105 AD, a Han court official refined how it was made.
By tradition, Chinese prisoners taught papermaking in Samarkand after a battle in 751.
By 794, Baghdad had a paper mill, and books multiplied across the Islamic world.
Paper reached Europe through Spain in the 1100s, centuries before the printing press.

scenes.purpose: Show that the routes also spread disease.

visual.title: A deadly passenger
visual.statement: In the 1340s, the Black Death likely moved west along trade routes into Europe.
points: A third or more of Europe dies

narration.text: The routes also carried something deadly.
In the 1340s, plague spread from Central Asia toward the Black Sea.
Fleas on rats, and on travelers, moved it from town to town.
Ships then carried it into Mediterranean ports,
and the Black Death killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people.

scenes.purpose: Show how traffic rose and fell with empires.

events.label: A sea route around Africa to India

narration.text: Traffic rose and fell with the empires along the way.
It boomed after Han China opened trade to the west, around 130 BC.
It flourished again under China's Tang dynasty, from the 600s to the 800s.
Under the Mongols, travel grew safer, and Marco Polo set out for the east in 1271.
But in 1498, Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India.
Ships could move far more, far more cheaply, and the overland routes slowly faded.

scenes.purpose: Explain why sea trade overtook caravans.

narration.text: Why did the sea win?
Caravans were slow, carried small loads and paid tolls at every border.
Ships carried huge cargoes in a single voyage and cut out many middlemen.

scenes.purpose: Summarize the lasting legacy.

visual.title: What the caravans left behind
visual.statement: The Silk Road tied distant peoples together long before anyone spoke of globalization.

narration.text: The caravans are gone, but their traces are everywhere.
Grapes and alfalfa traveled east into China, along with new foods and fashions.
Faiths, art and inventions mixed in the oasis cities.
In a real sense, the Silk Road was an early version of our connected world.

scenes.purpose: Note the modern recognition of the routes.

stats.label: of routes named a World Heritage Site in 2014
historic sites in China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan

narration.text: In 2014, UNESCO listed a stretch of about five thousand kilometers as a World Heritage Site.
It includes thirty-three sites across China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

scenes.purpose: Close with the main idea.

visual.title: More than a trade route
visual.statement: Every exchange on the Silk Road moved ideas, beliefs and risks along with the goods.

narration.text: So the next time you hear about global trade, picture those camel caravans.
Every exchange on the Silk Road moved more than goods.
It moved ideas, beliefs and even diseases, and it changed everyone it touched.
